segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Dave was in his late 20s, and it would not be accurate to say that he was living at home with his parents, but only because half the time he was staying at his sister's house. He was playing in a band, doing some writing, not making much money, and his parents were worried. And one day he was hanging out with his mom.

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: We were coming home from going ice skating together, which right there you can see that out. To be fair, I like ice skating. I'm a quarter Canadian.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait, wait, wait. You can see what? What does that show that you went ice skating with your mom?

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: Well, most guys, after a certain age, wouldn't go regularly ice skating with their mom to like [? organ ?] sessions where you're skating arm in arm around. I mean this is the sort of stuff I would do with my mom, like pretty regularly.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So they pull into the driveway. Dave's mom tells him there's going to be a benefit for this retirement home for nuns and priests. His mom's an old school Catholic who goes to mass every day. And she says it's going to be at a hotel in downtown Cleveland. They live in Cleveland. And Maureen McGovern, who sang the theme to The Poseidon Adventure back in the '70s was going to be the entertainment.

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: And she's like, so I'm getting tickets. So let me know if you want to go. And I said, no, I don't want to go. And then, so she just said, OK, well just let me know then. She's like, because I have to get the tickets in the next couple of weeks. And I figured, I didn't give it any thought, but then it kept coming up over and over. Like, let me know, the benefit's coming up and I need to buy tickets. So are you going to go? And I said, no. And she said, all right, well I need to know by next week if you're going to go. And this just went on and on for a couple of weeks.

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: This was a big thing. My mom kept saying like, and there will be nuns and priests there. Like they're going to get some of the old nuns and priests from the retirement place out. You can walk up and touch them and stuff. I don't know why she made that a selling point.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Maybe that was a selling point for her. Maybe she likes nuns and priests.

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: She does.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And she knows some of the old ones from back in the day.

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: Oh yeah, she's super into nuns and priests.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And these weren't just the regular nuns and priests that she see's everyday on the ball field. These are some of the older players. You have the cards, you know, but you never see out of the stadium anymore.

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: Yeah, exactly. It was like the fantasy league. Like Father Mackey from St. Anne's in 1952.

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: So there's a lot of that going on. And then, somewhere along the line, my mom brings up the fact that a priest that used to teach at my high school when I was there, Father Dennis, was recovering from two heart attacks. And so she's like, you know, I ran into Father Dennis up at church. And I was telling him about the benefit. And he was really into it. Yeah, I bet he would like to come to this benefit also. Why don't you bring him? And I was like, I'm not going. And she's like, well, I already told him you were going to call.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So Dave realizes he's trapped. Checkmate. He's going to have to at least call Father Dennis.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And Father Dennis, was he just like another teacher at the school or was he somebody who you especially liked?

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: I liked him. Yeah, I mean I knew him. He ran the choir. Yeah, I thought he was a great guy. He loaned me his guitar. He played guitar. So it wasn't like we had kept in touch or anything. You know, I had fond memories of him. But I hadn't seen him in years.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So he gets Father Dennis on the phone and they agree that Dave is going to pick him up and they'll attend the event together.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Comes the big day, it goes exactly as you might imagine a lunchtime fundraiser for retired nuns and priests in a hotel in downtown Cleveland with Maureen McGovern singing usually goes. Now there were a couple of wild card moments to the day that I'll run through quickly for you.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: First, Dave runs into a friend at the event from grade school-- now gay-- whose Dave mom is convinced that they should set up with one of Dave's sisters, even though Dave tries to keep explaining to her that Guy is gay.

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: And she thinks that I'm being mean, insulting him by calling him gay. I'm like, no, he's a gay man. That's fine. And just explain to me why it's not going to work out?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Second, the luncheon buffet turns out to be mostly fried foods. None of which can be eaten by Father Dennis, who's still recovering from his two heart attacks and requested a special low fat meal. Though Dave's mom has come prepared for this.

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: She sort of like, looks around real quickly and then reaches under the table. And she snuck in a bag of bread and like sandwich meats thinking that we could just make some sandwiches for him at the table. And I'm just horrified.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Father Dennis tells her very politely, thanks, but no. He doesn't want a sandwich. And eventually the waiters do arrange for him to get some sort of meal. At their table are some very old people, Dave's parents, Dave, and Father Dennis.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There's no drinking, which Dave says might have really helped things. And after a while, Dave and Father Dennis have run out of small talk.

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: So it's getting quiet and we're sitting next to each other. At some point, Father Dennis turns to me and he's sort of like, you know, I don't know. Normally I understand why I'm somewhere. If I'm invited somewhere I know why. But I guess I don't know. I don't know why I'm here. I'm really confused. I don't feel any connection to this. And I was just like, what? What do you mean? I thought you wanted to be here. I thought that was the whole thing. That's why I'm here. I thought you wanted to be here.

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: And he says, no. Your mother told me that you wanted to be here and that you really wanted me to go. So I thought that I should do it for you and your mom. And we're just sitting there, like oh gosh. We've been just duped by what I thought was a really nice lady.

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: My mother just tricked us into this.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Did you ask your mom afterwards about the whole thing?

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And did she explain what she was hoping was going to happen once she got you and Father Dennis together?

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: No, she just kept saying like, oh, I just thought it would be a really nice time for you. For both of you. She was very invasive about it. And I confronted her saying, do you think like that I'm going to hang out with his priest and then I'm going to want to become a priest? And she's like, no.

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: She wouldn't admit to that, and that's maybe--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But you think that's what it might be? Like in the back of her mind she's just like, maybe you're single, you're in your late 20s. Maybe you should be a priest?

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: Maybe. Or at least have some sort of like priestly influence. I think there was like a bigger thing, but she'll never tell me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Dave says this was par for the course. His mom often mystified him. And a certain amount of her parenting, of any parenting really, is putting your kids into situations you know are going to be good for them whether they like it or not. Or even, whether they understand it.

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: There's been a number of things over the years that I just could not wrap my head around why she was making me do it. And I really thought she was torturing me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Like what?

segments.speaker: Dave Hill
segments.text: She made me take typing lessons that I could not fathom why. I was like 13-years-old, 14-years-old. It just seemed just random, like here's something that I'll hate. I'll just make him do it. And like, now, literally like it didn't even hit me until like the last few years when I realized that a huge part of everyday for me, I'm typing all the time. I remember seeing that one day and be like, oh my God. That's why she made me endure that horrible summer of typing lessons. Literally, 20 years later I figured it out why she did that to me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today on our show, The Parent Trap, stories of parents doing their best to be good parents and do right by their kids by putting the kids into situation that they believe will be helpful. Our show in two acts today. Act one, Letter Day Saint. David Segal has the story of a mom doing something that you would expect and hope a mom would do, give her kid a little advice. Act two, The Opposite of Tarzan. We are very, very excited to have a brand new story from the amazing team that does the show Radiolab. This is a story about interspecies parenting. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act 1, Letter Day Saint.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Sometimes a parent can do something kind of extraordinary, really above and beyond what most people do with the best of intentions, just looking out for their kid. And do I even need to say that they can have all kinds of unintended consequences. David Segal has this example.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: In 1991, Elizabeth Gee was dying of cancer. And as she thought about the time she had left to live, she worried about her only child, Rebecca. Then 16 years old. And she discussed her worries with her husband.

segments.speaker: Gordon Gee
segments.text: She just looked at me one night. I mean, she was hooked up with all of this stuff.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: This is Gordon Gee.

segments.speaker: Gordon Gee
segments.text: And she just looked at me. She said, you know, I really feel that I need to continue to be an influence on Rebecca's life and continue to be part of her life. She knew she was terminal. She knew that she only had about a month to live. And she made this discrimination that she was going to write letters to her daughter.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: Specifically, birthday letters. The plan she told Gordon was this. She would write letters that he would send to Rebecca, one per year, every year, on December 4, Rebecca's birthday. The letters would be sealed and for Rebecca's eye's only. There were 13 of them. Each tailored for a specific birthday. Plus a letter for the day of Rebecca's wedding. Rebecca didn't know any of this until the first letter, which she read the day she turned 17.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: To a daughter reeling from the loss of her mother, it was the ultimate birthday present.

segments.speaker: Rebecca
segments.text: She said in one of my first letters that these were a way to connect to her. That all I had to do to connect to her was to open a letter. And then she would be there.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: One of the early letters arrived on a birthday at college, when she was feeling particularly isolated.

segments.speaker: Rebecca
segments.text: And this letter said basically, you will never be alone. You will never be alone. You will always have me. And I just remember feeling this incredible feeling of peace. It almost felt like getting a letter from someone who was alive.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: It happened the same way every year. Gordon, a college president for most of his professional life, now at Ohio State University, would overnight a sealed envelope, adding a brief card of his own. And every year, Rebecca went through a birthday letter ritual.

segments.speaker: Rebecca
segments.text: Usually sometime in the afternoon before dinner I'd sit down and open it and read Dad's note. Feel the page, look at her signature. Usually it'd be the first thing. And think, gosh, that's just so amazing that she's gone and I'm looking at her signature and it's saying I love you. And then I'd read through it.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: Each letter was about 2,000 typed words on thick white paper signed by hand, "You're the sweetest girl in the world. Or just, "Love forever, Mommy."

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: Elizabeth told Gordon that she wanted to describe the world as she saw it, and as Rebecca would see it as a young woman. And she does so in the letters with a mix of pep talks, moral instruction, autobiography, and parental affection. Often she focuses on what was happening to her on the age Rebecca would be when she opened each letter.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: So when Rebecca turned 21, Elizabeth described a dress she owned when she was 21. Quote, "You would not believe what I wore. A black fake fur suit with a pink top and the plastic ping pong earrings. Everyone thought it was fashionable, but I laugh when I think of it."

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: A lot of the letters are advice on how to live. Quote, "Most children benefit from the simulation of daycare," she writes. Urging Rebecca not to give up her career when she has children. Quote, "You are not a uni-dimensional person. Under that balance, you will be frustrated."

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: And her mother had high expectations. In one letter she asks her daughter, "Are you contemplating a dissertation? Interviewing with scientific laboratories or NASA? Traveling to excited places?" Rebecca pushed herself to meet those expectations.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: In college when her friends were out drinking, she stayed in and studied. Other kids might have found this all a little too heavy, Rebecca found it inspiring.

segments.speaker: Rebecca
segments.text: For example, when I decided I didn't have the confidence to go to medical school and I wasn't going to do it, the letter that year basically said, you need to find ethical expression in your work.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: She ended up going to medical school.

segments.speaker: Rebecca
segments.text: There was just no way I could have become a banker in the setting of these letters. I mean not that bankers don't have ethical expression, but for most of college, I think I had this enormous sense of purpose that I had a responsibility to do something meaningful. Both to me and to other people.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: As galvanizing as these letters could be, they could also be upsetting. The first person to fully appreciate how upsetting they were was her father. He was the one who dealt with the fall out. He saw that keeping his promise to his wife meant causing his daughter emotional distress. And on her birthday.

segments.speaker: Gordon Gee
segments.text: It was as if I could predict the sunrising. Rebecca would get the letters and then, I'd receive either that night or the next morning, a very tearful telephone call about how much she missed her mom. And I'd have these prolonged telephone calls.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: What sort of things would you talk about?

segments.speaker: Gordon Gee
segments.text: Well, I mean, she'd just say she's sad. You know, very sad. I wish my mother had been able to live. And been able to be here for me when I needed her. And been able to go shopping with me and all the kinds of things that I think any young woman would love to have her mother do. And you can imagine, that was very difficult for me.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: Toward the end of her college years, the letters were difficult for Rebecca for another reason. One of her mother's regular theme, actually you could say it was the dominant theme, was religious faith. The Gee's are Mormons and to her mother, staying close to the church was essential.

segments.speaker: Rebecca
segments.text: The most important thing for her was that I be a Mormon woman in the way that she wanted me to be. Which was a woman that went to the temple. A woman who married a Mormon man. A woman who believed all of the Mormon theology.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: By the time Rebecca was a senior in college, she was moving away from the church. So she worried a lot about disappointing her mother, who in the letters was constantly imploring her to stay. Quote, "You must always have the goal of going to the temple. For there you receive great gifts. It is in the temple that we are joined in eternal bonds and powers that will unite us in the world's beyond."

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: In another letter she wrote, "You will make good life choices. I know you will. But no matter your choice, never lose sight of the temple for me, please."

segments.speaker: Rebecca
segments.text: By age 21, after a few years of getting these letters and going through a process where I realized this right not going to be in my life, sometimes I would feel angry. And I remember at age 21 thinking, man, do I have to open up this one this year? This is tough. I don't want to do it. And my friend saying, well, why don't you wait? We'll go out to dinner. Maybe open it up tomorrow. And I felt guilty. And I remember feeling like if I didn't open it up I would really disappoint her. And yet, then I open it up and it's all about, I hope you marry a Mormon man and I hope you go to the temple. And if you don't go to the temple, you won't go to heaven. You're not going to see me. And I'm not doing it. And that's a pretty hard thing to hear on your birthday.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: Gordon was devout, but he could listen to Rebecca's reasons for leaving the church and came to accept them. Her mother couldn't do that. And in the three-way conversation that is part of any relationship of child, mother, and father, the voice of Rebecca's mother always spoke the loudest. It might seem strange that the deceased parent had the most sway, but her mother's opinion was fixed. There's no arguing with her. That haunted Rebecca. And while Gordon found himself reassuring his daughter, the comforts he offered were always trumped by Rebecca's memory of her mother.

segments.speaker: Gordon Gee
segments.text: It's difficult to compete with a dead spouse or in this sense, a dead mother. Because I'm here and I have all of the frailties of who I am. And over time, obviously her mother became very iconic. In many ways, very perfect. And clearly, could do no wrong. And I mean I never did say this to her, although I've joked with her a couple times. You know, who am I, chopped liver?

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: Because the letters were written exclusively for Rebecca, Gordon thought it was inappropriate to ask too many questions about them. For the same reason, Rebecca never volunteered to share them. Father and daughter were just following a set of instructions. As outdated and as trying as those instructions were.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: Over the years, as he dealt with his daughter's anguish, Gordon tossed out some hints the perhaps it was a bad idea for him to lob these annual grief bombs into her life.

segments.speaker: Gordon Gee
segments.text: I did on several occasions, I just said, you know, you have to remember that your mother was very ill. And that she loved you very much. But I'm not quite certain how healthy this is to have these letters and I said that to her directly. And I've said that to her on several occasions. And because it was very hard on me. It would really break my heart when I would hear her be so sad.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: But Rebecca never seemed to pick up on her father's hints, or his misgivings. As painful as the letters were, she felt as though she had no choice but to read them carefully. So Gordon sent them all, though he was conflicted about it enough that he actually delegated the FedExing part to his secretary.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: All of this letter related dread culminated with Rebecca's wedding, which happened in 2006 in an Episcopal church. But Rebecca and Gordon suspected the letter Elizabeth wrote for Rebecca's wedding would contain her longest course yet on the importance of marrying in a Mormon temple. Which is why both father and daughter told me they were secretly relieved when the letter, which Gordon's secretary says she sent, vanished in the FedEx system.

segments.speaker: Rebecca
segments.text: I remember thinking, if there is one for my wedding, I definitely don't want to open it on my wedding day. Because I really want my wedding day to be happy. And I don't want to sit, I don't want to cry. That day in particular, didn't want the letter to be a part of it.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: Because all the birthday letters had been sent, the wedding letter would have been the final letter in the series.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: Was there part of you when the letters ran out that felt relief?

segments.speaker: Gordon Gee
segments.text: Yeah, I think so. I think that without a doubt, it was an opportunity to move on. On the other level, this was the last kind of visible written, tangible connection that she had with her mother.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: It's almost like another death?

segments.speaker: Gordon Gee
segments.text: Right. And I think it was to her in many ways.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: But it was also a new beginning. For the first time, Rebecca began living a life that wasn't shadowed by a looming reminder of her mother's unmet hopes. Rebecca had become a physician. And she married a doctor named Allan Moore, whom she had met in residency. It was a very happy marriage and it ended tragically, a mere 18 months after it started when the couple was hit by an SUV while riding a Vespa.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: Rebecca was severely injured and Allan was killed. For the second time in her life, Rebecca was forced to cope with a devastating loss. But this time was different. She spent her months of physical rehab contemplating and writing about her memories of Allan.

segments.speaker: Rebecca
segments.text: And I remember thinking to myself, this is how it should be when you grieve for someone. You should remember the beautiful times, the things you shared. You should celebrate that person, but you shouldn't be dragged back into the grave with them every year. Why did she do this to me?

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: Rebecca says a year and a half after her husband's death, she feels like she's farther along in her grieving for him than she was 10 years after her mother died.

segments.speaker: Rebecca
segments.text: I mourned my husband's loss, Allan's loss. I love him, but I'm moving on with my life as he would want me to. I think to have letters from him for my birthdays or a yearly, would make it harder for me to move on.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: At the same time, the letters her mother sent were so essential in forming the person that Rebecca became, it's hard for her to imagine growing up without them.

segments.speaker: Rebecca
segments.text: In the end, would I have wanted a life without these? I can't say that because they made me feel incredibly loved. They made me know how much she valued her time on this earth with me. I got to hear that. I got to hear that after she died.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: Recently, Rebecca has started to grasp the hardships the letters imposed on her dad. And she thinks it would've been better if she had shared the letters with her father in real time, even if that went against her mother's wishes. This surely wasn't Elizabeth's intention, but when she wrote those letter, she left behind the bricks for a wall that kept her husband and her daughter apart, at least when the subject came to Elizabeth. Along with instructions that made discussing that wall very difficult. It was a plan that neither Rebecca nor Gordon ever consented to. And now, very gingerly, the wall is being dismantled.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: A months ago Rebecca sent her Dad a copy of one of the letters from her 24th birthday. Much of which is about Gordon's strengths as a dad. She has yet to share any of the others. And during our interview, Gordon joked that he was a little jealous that I got to read the letters before he did.

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: But a dying wish has a momentum all its own. And though the letters are now locked in a safe in Gordon's home, he still hasn't looked at them. And Rebecca still hasn't asked him to.

segments.text: This day is the first day that I went actually on the island.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She pulled her boat up to the tip of the island where there's just a little clearing and she parked. And as she did, Lucy and the other chimps who had heard the boat, came out of the forest and into the clearing. And Lucy and her walked toward each other.

segments.speaker: Janice Carter
segments.text: And I took with me some of Lucy's possession that had been important to her, like her mirror. And she used to like to draw and books, just to see how she responded to it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And what did she do?

segments.speaker: Janice Carter
segments.text: Well she looked at the things. She looked at the book. She looked at herself in the mirror and she signed to herself in the mirror. Then all of a sudden she grabbed me. I mean really grabbed me. One arm circled all the way around me and she sort of held me really, really tight. It really made me breathless and I started crying. She started begin these soft little pants. And I'm still pretty certain what she was saying to me was it's OK. You know, it's all OK now.

segments.speaker: Jad Abumrad
segments.text: At that moment, somebody in Janice's boat snapped a picture of her and Lucy hugging. It's a picture that Charles Siebert printed in his book. And it's one of those images that when you see it, I don't know why, it just haunts you.

segments.speaker: Jad Abumrad
segments.text: Lucy has their head against Janice's chest and Janice has her arms around Lucy.

segments.speaker: Charles Siebert
segments.text: It's one of the more fraught moments. You have to just look at the picture. I mean it sort of made me want to write the book. Something about the complexity and the invertedness of that picture.

segments.speaker: Janice Carter
segments.text: After that, the other chimps had started to go. And she wanted to go with them. And she got up and she didn't turn back to look at me. She just kept walking. She wanted to go with the other chimps and she did.

segments.speaker: Jad Abumrad
segments.text: A year later, Janice went back to visit Lucy again. But when she got there, this time Lucy was gone.

segments.speaker: Janice Carter
segments.text: And I went to all the different places looking to see if we could find anything. And we did. We found her body.

segments.speaker: Jad Abumrad
segments.text: She was lying right near the place where Janice's cage had been, just a skeleton.

segments.speaker: Janice Carter
segments.text: Her skull and her hands and her feet were separated from the rest of her skeleton.

segments.speaker: Robert Krulwich
segments.text: So how did you know that that was her body?

segments.speaker: David Segal
segments.text: She had a split between her front teeth and she was very long. And there was nobody else missing.

segments.speaker: Jad Abumrad
segments.text: And maybe the saddest, strangest thing was that--

segments.speaker: Janice Carter
segments.text: We didn't find any signs of her skin or hair.

segments.speaker: Jad Abumrad
segments.text: It appeared that Lucy had been skinned.

segments.speaker: Charles Siebert
segments.text: And no one knows actually what happened. But because the hands were taken, which poachers do, they thought one of the conjectures which makes it really unbelievably tragic is that they think that Lucy, always the first to approach humans, just sort of guilelessly approached poachers, not knowing that they were that. And that they just took advantage of their unwitting and over eager prey. But that was Lucy's end.

segments.speaker: Janice Carter
segments.text: The scenario that I have developed to cope with her death is that a fisherman or someone, some local person that just happened to pull up next to the land and was going to take a break or [UNINTELLIGIBLE PHRASE] or do something. And because she always felt confidence around humans, she probably approached the person. Perhaps she surprised the person and just on reflexes, defense, she was probably shot. I've got no other explanation.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Janice Carter still lives in Gambia. It's then when she realized that the chimps there would never have a chance to survive unless their human neighbors understood that might be a good thing. So these days she spends a lot of her time teaching people in Gambia about chimps, to convince them about the importance of protecting the chimps habitat.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Charles Siebert's latest book, all about the midway point between animals and humans is The Wauchula Woods Accord.
